title: Scorpion
intro: Scorpion is a tracked ground robot with a 360-degree pan-tilt camera head, built as a platform for embodied AI. These are the design pages and simulation results from its development: drag the 3D pages to turn them. Reviewers of the research paper "Checks That Can Fail" can start with the first section, which follows the paper.

sections.name: For the paper's reviewers
sections.intro: These are the visuals behind the research plan "Checks That Can Fail", which asks how far AI-assisted design can be trusted when the checks that accept it can themselves be wrong. Its two-week pilot on this robot tested each kind of check with something outside it: planted faults for the CAD checks (H1), a simulator for the surrogate model (H2) and real hand drops for the simulator (H3). The items follow the paper in that order, each captioned with the claim it supports. The 3D pages further down can be turned with the mouse.

items.title: The paper: Checks That Can Fail
items.caption: The research plan these pages support: AI-assisted design is only as trustworthy as its checks, so each kind of check is tested (PDF, opens on GitHub).

items.title: Figure 1: the pilot's results
items.caption: Figure 1 of the paper: seeded faults caught (H1), the surrogate against the simulator (H2) and Brier scores against the real drops (H3).

items.title: H1: a real change behind a seeded fault
items.caption: A real change behind seeded fault M13: in set 11 the loose shelf ring of set 10 is part of the base, so it cannot fall out when the head is upside down.

items.title: A surrogate of the shape sweep
items.caption: H2: the Gaussian process standing in for the simulator, around the best design with a 95% band (the paper reports 90% intervals), and where the 400 simulated shapes sit.

items.title: H2: the surrogate in detail
items.caption: H2 in detail: picking the next design to simulate by the surrogate's uncertainty against picking at random, the surrogate against the simulator on held-out designs, and a map of the chance of landing upright. (the right panel's 'peak' is an edge-rounding setting, not a probability)

items.title: Simulation against real drops
items.caption: H3: what each contact model predicted against what 361 real hand drops did, at 6 and 30 cm; the Brier scores are in the panel titles.

items.title: Simulated drops
items.caption: H3: scale bodies dropped in MuJoCo, default floor beside bouncing floor; at 30 cm the bouncing floor scored a Brier score of 0.63 against 1.16 for the default.

items.title: H3: the first drop tally sheet
items.caption: H3: the pen-and-paper tally of the first 6 cm hand-drop session: three printed bodies, six starting positions, five drops each, one mark per landing.

items.caption: About 145,000 simulated shell shapes; the winners have one place to rest, on their wheels.

items.title: Step Trainer
items.licence: Shows the Raspberry Pi 5 model (Printables 727155, CC0), credited in THIRD_PARTY.md. The PCA9685 board and MG90S servo are stand-in boxes: their models' licences aren't recorded.
items.caption: The search's step layout built: smaller wheels closer together, the belly 54 mm up on drop-plate pods.

items.title: Driving down a step
items.caption: The Trainer and the step layout driving down the same 400 mm step in MuJoCo. In the step test (hard floor, 640 runs each) the Trainer ends upright in 51% of runs and the step layout in 63%; at 400 mm, 14% against 38%. This run is seed 1, the first where they differ.

items.title: Four wheels against six on rough ground
items.caption: Four wheels against six on a ridge with 40-degree sides and over gaps: the four-wheel belly touches the ridge, the six-wheel body clears it by 2 mm at worst, and both cross gaps up to 70 mm.
